title: AustralianSuper targets $20bn private credit portfolio
full_text:
AustralianSuper’s reported plan to grow its private credit portfolio to almost $20 billion within four years reflects more than a push into an increasingly popular asset class; it signals how Australia’s largest superannuation fund is repositioning its investment strategy as more members enter retirement.
According to reporting from the Australian Financial Review, AustralianSuper plans to almost double its private credit exposure to around $20 billion over the next four years before expanding the portfolio further over the longer term.
The strategy comes as the fund argued Australia’s super system is entering a new phase, with investment portfolios needing to deliver not only long-term capital growth but also more predictable income for a growing cohort of retirees.
Head of fixed income, currency and credit Katie Dean said Australia’s retirement system had historically focused on accumulation, but that was changing as more members began drawing an income from their super.
Dean said around 1.6 million Australians aged over 65 were now drawing an income from super, with the Treasury forecasting that figure would rise to around 2.5 million over the next decade.
“This is not simply a demographic observation; it changes the shape of the investment task,” she said. “As more members move into decumulation, super funds need to think not only about maximising long-term growth, but also about how portfolios manage risk to deliver more predictable income streams and support members throughout retirement.”
Against that backdrop, AustralianSuper has broadened its approach to credit investing by bringing private credit into its wider fixed income portfolio, allowing investment opportunities to be assessed across public and private markets rather than in isolation. This reflected the fund’s belief that credit should be viewed as a single investment universe.
“Credit is a broad and diverse asset class, spanning public and private markets,” she said. “The change will allow us to assess opportunities across the credit spectrum more effectively, with a more integrated approach to portfolio construction, including how different forms of credit work together.
“As Australia’s credit market deepens, we believe a more integrated approach to credit investing is the best way to access those opportunities.”
The expansion also comes as regulators and market participants scrutinise the rapid growth of private credit. Dean acknowledged concerns around leverage, lending standards and borrowers’ ability to manage higher interest rates, but said those risks varied considerably across the market.
“Successful investing in private credit starts with disciplined underwriting, strong loan structures, appropriate diversification and careful manager selection,” she said.
“We focus on how capital is protected in downside scenarios and believe successful private credit investing is driven as much by avoiding losses as it is by generating income.”
AustralianSuper is also expanding its global credit capability, with investment teams across Australia, the UK and the US supported by specialist external managers.
Dean said the fund’s evolving strategy was no longer centred on deciding how much credit to hold, but rather identifying which forms of credit were best suited to different investment objectives and market conditions.
As part of that approach, AustralianSuper expects to invest across a wider range of credit sectors, including leveraged loans, high-yield bonds, investment-grade credit and private credit, each offering different combinations of income, liquidity and risk.
The fund believes Australia’s credit market is also becoming deeper and more diverse, creating additional opportunities for institutional investors while broadening funding options for Australian businesses.
“A deeper credit market benefits both the Australian economy and long-term investors,” Dean said. “For investors, a broader and more liquid credit market expands the opportunity set and provides greater access to income-producing investments.”
